title: Microservice boundaries
subtitle: Decide which parts of an application need separate services.
description: Compare modular monoliths and microservices, then define service boundaries and data ownership. Learn HTTP communication, timeouts, and independently deployable contracts.

lessons.title: Modular monolith or microservices?
lessons.summary: Microservices offer independent deployment and scaling at the cost of distributed-system complexity.
objectives: Identify a concrete reason to separate a service.
keyPoints: Independent deployment and scaling are benefits, not automatic outcomes.
A modular monolith keeps boundaries without adding network calls.
Services that must always deploy together may form a distributed monolith.
practice: Write an ADR comparing a modular monolith with separate Order and Inventory services.
The decision names a business or operational need and its costs.

exercises.prompt: Which are primary benefits of microservices?
options: A service can deploy without redeploying every other service.
A heavily used service can scale independently.
Network calls are faster than method calls.
Data consistency automatically becomes easier.
exercises.explanation: Independent deployment and scaling are possible benefits. Network failures and distributed consistency add operational work.

exercises.prompt: Three developers are building a new product with an unclear domain. Which starting point is most reasonable?
options: A modular monolith with clear boundaries, splitting later if a real need appears.
Twelve microservices immediately.
One giant class without modules.
One service per database table.
exercises.explanation: Boundaries are easier to refine within a codebase before committing to separate deployments and network contracts.

lessons.title: Domain boundaries & data ownership
lessons.summary: Group services around business capabilities and give each data set one owner.
objectives: Access another service’s data through its contract.
keyPoints: Table boundaries alone rarely define a useful service.
Only the owning service should write its data.
Shared internal schemas create hidden contracts between services.
practice: Assign ownership of orders, stock, reservations, and notification records.
Order accesses Inventory through an API or events rather than direct SQL.

exercises.prompt: Order needs available stock. Which approach preserves Inventory ownership?
options: Call Inventory’s API or consume its stock events.
Query Inventory’s stock table directly.
Copy its internal stock table with a nightly SQL script.
Give Order write access to Inventory’s stock table.
exercises.explanation: An API or event contract lets Inventory change its internal schema without requiring Order to change.

exercises.prompt: Which signs suggest an unsuitable service boundary?
options: Every feature changes Order and Inventory and requires a coordinated release.
One user request triggers six synchronous service calls.
Each service has its own database.
Inventory can release without waiting for Order.
exercises.explanation: Repeated coordinated changes and long synchronous chains suggest tight coupling rather than independent services.

lessons.title: Synchronous communication contracts
lessons.summary: HTTP calls need explicit timeouts and useful mappings from downstream failures to domain errors.
objectives: Map downstream failures to application responses.
keyPoints: Use Boot’s RestClient.Builder so instrumentation is preserved.
Connect and read timeouts bound different parts of a request.
Long synchronous dependency chains reduce end-to-end availability.
practice: Create an Inventory client with a configured base URL and a two-second read timeout.
A slow dependency produces a bounded, clearly reported failure.

exercises.prompt: Create an Inventory RestClient bean using the configured base URL and a two-second read timeout with SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory.
exercises.explanation: Connect timeout bounds connection setup; read timeout bounds waiting for response data.

exercises.prompt: Order, Inventory, and Payment each have 99% availability and all are required synchronously. What is approximate combined availability, assuming independent failures?
options: About 97%
100%, because there are three services
exercises.explanation: 0.99 cubed is about 0.9703. Every required dependency adds another potential point of failure.

lessons.title: Independent deployment & data
lessons.summary: Independent releases need stable contracts, backward compatibility, and enforced data ownership.
keyPoints: A new provider version must still support running consumers.
Additive changes can ease migration before removing old fields.
Separate schemas and users can enforce ownership on one database server.
practice: Rename a field through a compatible transition and restrict each database user to its own schema.
Old consumers continue working during rollout.

exercises.prompt: Inventory replaces qty with available. Order the compatible release steps.
items: Inventory returns both qty and available.
Confirm no consumer still reads qty.
exercises.explanation: Expand the contract first, migrate consumers, and only then remove the old field.

exercises.prompt: Order and Inventory share one PostgreSQL server for a lab. How can ownership still be enforced?
options: Use separate schemas and users; Order’s user cannot access Inventory’s schema.
Use one schema and user and rely on a verbal agreement.
Put every service’s JSON in one data table.
Ignore ownership while the app runs.
exercises.explanation: Sharing a database process can be practical, but database permissions should enforce the service boundaries.
